displayQuote: In the unlikely story that is America, there has never been anything false about hope

meta.title: Who really said "In the unlikely story that is America, there has never been anything false about hope"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, Obama said it — on New Hampshire primary night, 8 January 2008 in Nashua. Not the Iowa caucus speech, and the wording is often quietly clipped.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'In the unlikely story that is America, there has never been anything false about hope'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Barack Obama, New Hampshire primary night, 8 January 2008 — a direct answer to the charge that he was selling 'false hopes.'

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: Born 1961 · 44th U.S. president; U.S. senator from Illinois in January 2008
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and precisely locatable: Obama said it on New Hampshire primary night, 8 January 2008, conceding to Hillary Clinton at Nashua High School South — the speech remembered as “Yes We Can.” The line was a direct answer to the Clinton campaign’s charge that he was selling “false hopes,” which is why it lands as a rebuttal rather than a platitude.

source.excerpt: We’ve been warned against offering the people of this nation false hope. But in the unlikely story that is America, there has never been anything false about hope.
source.trailTitle: How the line came to be said
trail: 4 January 2008 — the setup. Campaigning in New Hampshire days after losing Iowa, Hillary Clinton sharpened the contrast Obama would answer, arguing that America needed someone who could “actually deliver change,” not “false hopes” ↗. “False hope” was her campaign’s word, not his.

3 January 2008 — not here. Obama’s Iowa caucus victory speech is the one people half-remember, and it does contain a hope passage — “Hope is not blind optimism” ↗ — but the American Presidency Project’s transcript contains neither “false hope” nor “the unlikely story that is America.” The famous line was still five days away.

8 January 2008 — the line. Beaten in New Hampshire, Obama conceded at Nashua High School South. Contemporaneous transcripts of the primary-night speech carry the sentence intact and in order, immediately after the “false hope” setup and immediately before the “Yes we can” refrain — see the January 2008 transcript ↗.

February 2008 — it becomes a song. will.i.am’s viral video turned the speech into music: Wikipedia records that the lyrics are entirely quotations from the New Hampshire concession speech ↗, written by then-speechwriter Jon Favreau. That video is how most people met the words — and how they got separated from the night that produced them.
source.excerptNote: The first sentence is the half almost always dropped. Without it the line reads as a slogan; with it, it is a rebuttal — Obama is turning a specific attack word back on the people using it.

author.name: Barack Obama
author.heading: Who said it
author.metaLine: Born 1961 · 44th U.S. president; U.S. senator from Illinois in January 2008
author.bio: Barack Obama was a first-term U.S. senator from Illinois when he delivered this line, eight days into the 2008 primary calendar and fresh off an upset win in Iowa followed by an upset loss in New Hampshire. His campaign rhetoric was built around hope as an argument rather than a mood — a theme his rivals attacked as naive, and which he defended by rooting it in American history. He went on to win the Democratic nomination and the presidency, serving from 2009 to 2017.

misattribution.heading: What gets it wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — Obama really said this. What goes wrong is everything around it: the wrong speech, a clipped wording, and no source at all.

items.who: The Iowa caucus victory speech, 3 January 2008
items.why: Easily the most common error, repeated by aggregators and search summaries alike. Obama’s Iowa caucus-night remarks are a hope speech — they contain “Hope is not blind optimism” ↗ — but the American Presidency Project transcript has neither “false hope” nor “the unlikely story that is America” anywhere in it. Right theme, wrong night, five days early.

items.who: “there’s never been anything false about hope”
items.why: A contraction creeps in. Quotes.net renders the line as “there’s never been anything false about hope” ↗; the transcripts read “there has never been.” Minor, but it is the tell of a quote copied from another quote site rather than from a transcript.

The Goodreads entry ↗ carries the line with the author’s name and topic tags — “america,” “history,” “hope” — and no speech, no date, no citation. A genuine quote with no provenance attached is how a genuine quote eventually becomes a doubtful one.

misattribution.truthLine: The real address: New Hampshire primary night, 8 January 2008, Nashua — sourced in Wikiquote’s entry for the “Yes, we can” speech ↗, and preserved in the contemporaneous transcripts of that night.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Obama lost that night. The polls had shown him winning New Hampshire comfortably after Iowa; Clinton took it 39.1% to 36.5%, and the speech he gave was a concession. That is the fact most often stripped away when the line is quoted — it reads as a victory lap, but it was written to be delivered from behind.

It was also an argument, not an aphorism. For a week the Clinton campaign had been hammering the word “false hopes” at him as a charge of naivety. Obama took the attack word, put it in the mouth of his critics in one sentence, and turned it over in the next. The rhetorical move is the whole point of the line, and it only works if you keep the sentence before it.
detailsBody: The speech is the origin of the “Yes we can” refrain as a campaign signature — the hope sentence is its immediate setup, the pivot from defense into the call-and-response that closes the speech.

A month later will.i.am built a viral music video entirely out of this speech’s words. That video carried the language far past anyone who had watched primary night, which is a plausible reason the words are now remembered as free-floating Obama inspiration rather than as a specific answer to a specific opponent on a specific losing night.
context.pull: He said it the night he lost.
